title: Oral History Collection: Voices from the Remnants — Arrivals in the GLMZ
body:
# Oral History Collection: Voices from the Remnants — Arrivals in the GLMZ

*The following testimonies were collected between 2218 and 2221 by the Vellichor Institute's Diaspora Documentation Project. Subjects were interviewed in their current GLMZ communities. All names have been changed at subjects' request. The Institute acknowledges that this collection represents a self-selected sample: people who made the journey and stayed. It does not represent people who returned, people who could not leave, or the majority of Remnant populations who never considered leaving.*

---

**Testimonial 1: Amara K., age 44. Origin: Cleveland, Ohio (Remnant). Current residence: Zone 7 Gray Zone.**

People ask me what Cleveland is like and they expect a certain kind of answer. They expect me to say it's terrible or it's beautiful or it's a place of terrible beauty, because that's the story they've already written. Cleveland is — it's a city. It has approximately 800,000 people. It has a functioning municipal government that holds elections and fixes the roads and runs the water system. It has hospitals. It has schools where teachers show up. I grew up there. My family is still there. My grandmother has never left Ohio and she is eighty-one years old and entirely fine.

I came to the GLMZ because there was a job. That's the whole story. I was recruited — Silkworm Data runs a recruitment program in the Remnants, they don't publicize it, but they find people with specific technical skills. I had the skills. They offered me a Tier 2 classification, housing in Zone 7, and a salary that I could not have earned in Cleveland in three years of work. I accepted. That's it.

Do I miss Cleveland? Yes. Is the GLMZ better? That depends entirely on what you value. If you value having a place in the tier system and access to the Pulse and the augmentation clinics and the kind of density that makes cities feel alive — then yes. If you value knowing your neighbors' names and a government that works for you instead of for shareholders and the feeling of being a person with full legal standing rather than a classified asset — then I'll tell you that Cleveland has things the GLMZ does not.

---

**Testimonial 2: Domingo F., age 31. Origin: Los Angeles, California (Remnant). Current residence: Zone 2 corponation territory (Rictus Entertainment employee).**

I grew up in Silver Lake, which is one of the neighborhoods that didn't burn. We had water — we had a desalination hookup, the community had organized one in 2108, before I was born. We weren't living in ruins. People think Los Angeles is ruins. Parts of it are ruins. Parts of it are extremely pleasant.

I left because I wanted to work in entertainment and the entertainment industry is in the GLMZ. Not all of it — there are independent producers in LA, there are artists, there is a scene — but the scale I wanted to work at requires Rictus or Waxwing. You can't make a Rictus budget production from LA. You could try. The talent is here, the infrastructure is here, the distribution pipeline is here. So I came here.

The thing I wasn't prepared for is how much of the GLMZ is the corponation territory and how much of it is not. I have a Tier 3 classification and I live in Rictus housing and I have access to things I couldn't have imagined in LA and I am also, meaningfully, an employee of Rictus Corponation in a way that has implications for my daily life that I'm still understanding. In LA I was a person who made things. Here I am a person who makes things for Rictus. Those are different situations. I'm not complaining. I'm describing.

---

**Testimonial 3: Nkechi O., age 67. Origin: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (Remnant). Current residence: Zone 3 Gray Zone.**

Philadelphia is not underwater. People from the GLMZ always think Philadelphia is underwater. The waterline runs through parts of South Philadelphia and the Delaware waterfront — those areas, yes, there's flooding at high tide, there are neighborhoods you don't go into at high water. But the rest of the city is a city. It is a city that looks like a city from 2050, because it is a city that hasn't had significant infrastructure investment since 2050, but it functions.

I came to the GLMZ forty years ago. I was twenty-seven. I came because my partner was here and I was not going to be separated from my partner by the fact of the Corridor's sponsorship system. That was the reason. She had gotten a Tier 2 classification and I was in the Remnants and there was no mechanism for me to follow her except to come and figure it out from inside.

What nobody tells you when you come from the Remnants is that entry is the easy part. You can enter the Gray Zone without a sponsor. The Gray Zone is outside the corponation territories — it's inside the GLMZ geographically but it's not sponsored territory. So you can get in. What you cannot do is access corponation services without a sponsor, and without a sponsor you are in the Gray Zone indefinitely. I spent eleven months in the Zone 3 Gray Zone before my partner's sponsorship came through. Those eleven months were the hardest of my life. They were also the most interesting. I know this neighborhood. I know the people in this neighborhood. I have lived here for forty years because when the sponsorship came through, I made the decision to stay.

---

**Testimonial 4: Jin-ho C., age 22. Origin: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (Remnant). Current residence: Zone 1 (Tessera Corponation employee).**

I won the exam. That's what we called it at home — winning the exam. The Vellichor Institute admits Remnant applicants by examination, and the acceptance rate is — I don't know the exact number, but my school had 400 students and I was the only one who passed, in the year I applied. My parents threw a party. People brought food. The neighbors came. People cried.

I arrived at Chicago Station and I stood in the concourse and I looked at the Pulse departure board and I understood for the first time that this was real. In Pittsburgh, the Pulse is something that other people have. You know it exists. You have seen it from the outside — there is a Pulse spur that passes through the eastern Pennsylvania corridor and you can see the infrastructure from the highway if you know where to look. But it is not something that is for you. It is a pipe that something passes through on its way between places that matter.

And then I was at Chicago Station and the board showed departures for Rotterdam and Lagos and Osaka and I had a ticket in my hand for Zone 3, which is where Vellichor is, and I was twenty years old and I had won the exam and I did not know yet what that meant or what I was becoming, only that the pipe was now for me, and that the fact of that was the biggest thing that had ever happened to me, and that I was not sure whether to be proud or terrified.

I am, four years later, both.
